title: The Trial Of Leslie Knope

jokes.text: Ron explaining the cookie ad situation: 'I was trying to buy this hand-crafted mahogany wood model of a B-25 Mitchell Panchito aircraft.'
jokes.setup: Ron is asking April a tech question, opening with what sounds like it could be a simple explanation.
jokes.punchline: The absurd specificity of the item — a hand-crafted mahogany model of a B-25 Mitchell Panchito — is perfectly on-brand for Ron and instantly funny before any punchline is delivered.
jokes.explanation: The joke is almost entirely in the character specificity. Only Ron Swanson would be shopping for this exact item, and the hyper-precise name of the aircraft is the comedic payload. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's so great, Ron. I'm really happy for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No, you're not.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, I'm not.

jokes.text: April: 'Aw, for me?' / Ron: 'Don't sass me.'
jokes.setup: Ron mentions the model airplane in a way that could theoretically be a gift.
jokes.punchline: April's mock-sweet 'for me?' followed by Ron's immediate, flat 'Don't sass me' — a perfect encapsulation of their relationship dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Three words of setup, three words of punchline. Maximum economy. The comedic rhythm of this exchange is perfectly timed and deeply character-specific — April's deadpan provocation and Ron's non-negotiable bluntness.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't understand. How do they know I looked at boat shoes online?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Cookies. They track your browsing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Cookies? I didn't eat any cookies.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, it's not actual cookies. It's data.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Then why would they call it that? That's a lie. I hate this.

jokes.text: Ron: 'So it learns information? About me? That seems like an invasion of privacy.'
jokes.setup: April explains browser cookies — a mundane tech concept.
jokes.punchline: Ron's genuine alarm at a completely standard internet function, framed as a principled libertarian outrage.
jokes.explanation: Ron's anti-government, anti-surveillance worldview colliding with basic internet functionality is a well-worn premise for the character but lands cleanly here.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh, and the government is also tracking your location through your phone.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: WHAT?!

jokes.text: April: 'Dude, if you think that's bad, go to Google Earth and type in your address.'
jokes.setup: Ron is scandalized by cookies tracking his name.
jokes.punchline: April, with maximum casual cruelty, directs him to something that will cause him to spiral into even greater privacy-related existential crisis.
jokes.explanation: April's line is perfectly calibrated: she says it with zero malice but full knowledge of what it will do to Ron. The structure is excellent — it's a punchline that also sets up an implied second joke we never see but can fully imagine. Economy is great.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ben and Leslie? That's... I mean, wow. Ben's usually into these really intense, driven, ambitious women. Leslie is basically a golden retriever in a blazer.

jokes.text: Character's talking head: 'I am, of course, shocked... And not just because Ben usually prefers tall brunettes.'
jokes.setup: The speaker expresses shock at Ben and Leslie's relationship.
jokes.punchline: The qualifier '...and not just because Ben usually prefers tall brunettes' — implying the shock has multiple layers, with the dating-type observation being the funnier secondary reason.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection structure works well — the 'not just because' reframe is a classic comedy technique deployed cleanly. Character integration is limited since we can't identify the speaker definitively.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm trying to help you up.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: From what? I'm standing.

jokes.text: Chris asks 'Are you hugging me, or are we fighting?' as he and Leslie/Ben appear to embrace awkwardly.
jokes.setup: Chris genuinely loves these two people and is trying to convey complicated emotions while also prosecuting them.
jokes.punchline: His earnest confusion about whether the physical contact is an embrace or a confrontation captures his bizarre emotional openness perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chris Traeger — his inability to separate his profound warmth from his institutional duties creates a genuinely funny collision. The binary 'hugging or fighting' framing is sharp and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know what? I think we're all going to feel a lot better after we get through this ethics investigation.

jokes.text: Chris describes Leslie and Ben as 'exemplary government employees,' and they both enthusiastically agree ('That's the word we were thinking of!' / 'Isn't it?').
jokes.setup: Chris is about to deliver bad news and is softening the blow with a compliment.
jokes.punchline: Leslie and Ben immediately forget the context and just enjoy the compliment, chiming in proudly as if they'd just been given an award rather than are about to face an ethics trial.
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble beat. Leslie's compulsive need for validation and Ben's quiet pride both shine. The timing of them agreeing with their own compliment before Chris gets to the bad news is a nice structural flourish.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I arrived early for my hearing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's 3 AM.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. Early!

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Then don't say it.' (in response to Chris saying 'which makes what I'm about to say even sadder')
jokes.setup: Chris is building up to announcing the ethics trial.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's flat, completely sincere 'Then don't say it' — as if that's a viable option.
jokes.explanation: Short and functional. The comedy is in Leslie genuinely meaning it — she's not being flip, she sincerely wishes he wouldn't. Economy is its greatest asset.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I tried to get here early, but... you can't out-early Leslie Knope. It's impossible. She's like a golden retriever mixed with a hurricane.

jokes.text: Leslie arrived at 3:00 A.M. for a hearing that starts at 8:30 A.M. Ben calls this 'an absurd pipe dream' that he thought he could get there before her.
jokes.setup: Ben mentions he wanted to sneak in before Leslie to set something up.
jokes.punchline: She arrived at 3 A.M. — five and a half hours early. Ben recognizing this as 'an absurd pipe dream I now realize was impossible' is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Pure Leslie character comedy. The joke requires no exaggeration — Leslie arriving at 3 A.M. is exactly what she would do. Ben's resigned acceptance of this reality ('an absurd pipe dream I now realize was impossible') is the perfect reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for this Li'l Sebastian toy!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You're welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're the best. I love you so much.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I love you too.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Leslie was talking to the toy.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: But also Ben.

jokes.text: Leslie receives the Li'l Sebastian stuffed animal from Ben and says 'Aw, thank you so much for making my life so wonderful.' Then immediately clarifies: 'I was talking to him. But also to you.'
jokes.setup: Ben gives Leslie a small stuffed Li'l Sebastian horse as a gift before the trial.
jokes.punchline: Leslie addresses her thanks to the toy first, then graciously includes Ben as an afterthought.
jokes.explanation: This lands on multiple levels simultaneously: it's a callback to Li'l Sebastian (a beloved running element), it's character-specific to Leslie's almost religious reverence for the miniature horse, AND it's a sweet/funny moment in a relationship beat. The structure is perfect — the clarification 'I was talking to him' is the surprise, and 'But also to you' rescues the moment warmly. High quotability. Ben's 'Of course' and 'Thanks' are the ideal reactions.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: If I get in trouble for this, I swear I'll die. Actually, no, I won't die. I'll just wish I was dead. Which is worse because then I have to live with the disappointment.

jokes.text: Ben describes himself as a 'wrinkled, hideous monster' in telling Leslie to look at the wall where he'll be sitting.
jokes.setup: Ben is giving Leslie an emotional send-off before the trial, telling her to look at the wall if she misses him.
jokes.punchline: He then immediately describes his own face as a 'wrinkled, hideous monster' — a shocking self-deprecating pivot in an otherwise tender moment.
jokes.explanation: The joke subverts what's meant to be a romantic gesture. Ben punctuating his own tenderness with casual self-loathing is funny and character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm a wrinkled, hideous monster.

jokes.text: The plaque about Marcus Everett Langley: his nickname 'Old Stone Face' was both due to his steely demeanor AND because 'dynamite blew up his face' at a rock quarry.
jokes.setup: Leslie reads an inspirational plaque about a historical Pawnee lawyer.
jokes.punchline: The nickname 'Old Stone Face' has a heroic explanation — steely demeanor — immediately undercut by the literal one: an accident blew up his face.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent joke construction. The setup implies a dignified metaphorical explanation and then delivers a brutally literal one with no fanfare. 'Dynamite blew up his face' is the kind of deadpan historical absurdism Parks does at its best — specific, unexpected, and delivered completely straight. The two-beat structure (demeanor / rock quarry accident) is near-perfect. Earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So why do they call him 'The Hammer'?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, it's because he's very aggressive in court. He just hammers away at witnesses, hammers the opposing counsel...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, that makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, no. The real reason is he has a claw hammer collection and he once threatened to use one on a judge.

jokes.text: Chris greets Leslie at the ethics trial by saying 'It is snowing outside. Isn't that great?' with exuberant joy while simultaneously saying he is 'quite miserable' about the trial.
jokes.setup: Chris has to run the ethics trial against someone he admires.
jokes.punchline: His compulsive positivity is so hardwired that he announces snow with joy immediately before revealing profound internal sadness.
jokes.explanation: Solid Chris character work. The juxtaposition of his physical radiance with his stated misery is his core comedic contradiction, deployed well here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chris, you say you're miserable, but you're smiling.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm not smiling, I'm in pain. I tried that herbal remedy you suggested.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Which one? The turmeric blend? The activated charcoal?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: All of them. I mixed them together. My mouth tastes like a forest fire mixed with wet gym socks.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... not ideal.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It gets worse. Then I added the ginger root, the cayenne pepper, and that mysterious powder you said was 'basically magic.'

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Now my mouth feels like a spaceship.

jokes.text: Chris explains his extreme good mood despite distress: two B-12 shots, 'an unreasonable amount of St. John's wort,' bee pollen paste rubbed around his gums, and 'now my mouth feels like a spaceship.'
jokes.setup: Leslie notices Chris seems too happy given the circumstances.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of herbal interventions culminates in 'my mouth feels like a spaceship' — a surreal image delivered with absolute clinical earnestness.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The escalation through three increasingly weird wellness interventions builds to 'my mouth feels like a spaceship' — an image that is both perfectly absurd and completely specific to Chris's character. Only Chris Traeger would say this. High quotability. The follow-up about maintaining 'extremely high dosages of herbal remedies' or getting depressed 'right now' extends the joke beautifully. This earns its 8.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, throughout history, there have been people willing to accept unjust punishment for their beliefs. Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., Joan of Arc...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I would be willing to go to jail for showing my elbow.

jokes.text: Chris: 'And stress leads to depression. And if I don't maintain an extremely high dosage of herbal remedies, I will get very depressed.' then: 'It's happening right now.'
jokes.setup: Chris has just explained his wellness regimen.
jokes.punchline: The immediate, real-time crash — 'It's happening right now' — suggesting his emotional state is moment-to-moment dependent on bee pollen.
jokes.explanation: The punchline of the previous joke's extended setup. 'It's happening right now' is extremely well-placed and earns big because of the structure built before it. The instantaneousness of his crash is the comedic payload.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was at the Ice Town press conference. Ben had just announced that Ice Town was a bad idea, and I realized I was in love with him. So I kissed him. It was a Tuesday. Actually, it was a Thursday. No wait, it was definitely a Tuesday because I remember I had eaten a turkey sandwich for lunch, and I only eat turkey on Tuesdays. Well, I eat turkey other days too, but that day it was specifically a turkey sandwich, not a wrap, and it had mustard—spicy mustard, not yellow mustard. Anyway, the point is, it was magical and perfect and everyone was watching and I didn't care because I was in love. I'm doing it again, aren't I? Oversharing?

jokes.text: Leslie, in explaining her historical inspiration, describes Sarah Nelson Quindle being 'set adrift on Lake Michigan like a human popsicle.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is drawing inspiration from a 19th century woman who accepted unjust punishment nobly.
jokes.punchline: 'Set adrift on Lake Michigan like a human popsicle' — an absurdly casual, almost whimsical description of what is essentially execution by hypothermia.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'human popsicle' is the gem here — a perfectly calibrated piece of dark comedy that trivializes horrific punishment in an almost cheerful way. Classic Pawnee historical absurdism. Leslie delivering it with earnest admiration for the woman's composure makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No! I would never ask for special treatment. I'm a public servant. I believe in following the rules and treating everyone equally.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, they're asking if you've ever used your position to get personal benefits.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh! Personal benefits! No, no, no. I mean, yes, sometimes I park in the handicapped spot, but only because my car is very large and I need the extra space. And occasionally I'll expense my lunch to the Parks Department, but I eat it at my desk while working, so it's basically a work meal. And sure, I had the city pay for my dental work, but I was eating city food, so it was their responsibility.

jokes.text: Leslie, describing when she and Ben first kissed: 'We kissed each other on each other's mouths. It was excellent.' Then: 'That was unnecessary to add. I'm sorry. I'm nervous.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving formal testimony and describes the beginning of the relationship.
jokes.punchline: 'We kissed each other on each other's mouths' — redundant specification — followed by the enthusiastic 'It was excellent,' then her own horrified self-correction.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best standalone joke. 'Kissed each other on each other's mouths' is a wonderfully strange redundancy that reveals Leslie's brain misfiring under stress. 'It was excellent' is a perfect awkward overshare. Then her immediate self-awareness — 'That was unnecessary to add. I'm sorry. I'm nervous.' — compounds it beautifully. Three comedic beats in rapid succession, all character-specific, all natural. High quotability. Could only be Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, I need you to get me evidence from the warehouse.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yes! Absolutely! I'm on it!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You don't even know what I'm asking you to do.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Doesn't matter. I'm ready to go. Let's do this!

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I received adorable nicknames and amazing back rubs.' (when asked if she received special treatment from Ben as her superior)
jokes.setup: The official question is about professional special treatment — favoritism, advantages, etc.
jokes.punchline: Leslie answers with personal/romantic benefits before catching herself: 'Oh, you mean professionally. No.'
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection structure — the professional context is established, Leslie answers on a completely different axis, then snaps back. 'Adorable nicknames and amazing back rubs' is a highly specific and endearing answer that tells us something real about the relationship while being funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, I need you to follow these instructions very carefully. First, go to the filing cabinet, open the second drawer, and pull out the folder marked 'Q'. Then bring it directly to my office. Do not stop, do not look in the folder, do not talk to anyone. Got it?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, I got it. Second drawer, folder Q, your office. Easy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, I'm serious. This is important.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, I know. I'm on it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Andy, where you going?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Leslie needs me to... uh... do something with a... thing. Actually, I have no idea what I'm doing. You wanna get lunch?

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Andy, I need evidence.' Gives detailed instructions. 'Where are you looking? Look here, focus here.' The implication that Andy immediately stopped paying attention.
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving Andy critical instructions while under trial pressure.
jokes.punchline: She has to redirect his attention mid-instruction — he's already zoned out.
jokes.explanation: A nice physical/visual beat — we can infer Andy is looking at something else entirely. Competent character comedy but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you're the Parks Director. How do you not know the other department heads?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I prefer to keep my interactions to a minimum. Less talking, more doing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But they work in the same building! Ann, back me up here.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, Ron, it's kind of your job to know who these people are.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know who they are. I just don't know their names or faces.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Those are the two main ways to know someone!

jokes.text: Andy's eagerness to get 'evidence' before knowing what evidence Leslie needs — she has to stop him: 'Wait! You don't know what evidence!'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Andy she needs evidence.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately bolts — pure enthusiastic incompetence, no information whatsoever.
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy — all enthusiasm, no information processing. The joke is in the implication of what he was about to do. The 'Ah, right on. Yes. Hit me.' recovery is a nice character touch.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: History will remember me as the woman who got things done.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I don't know the names of the other department heads.' Leslie and Ann stare. Ann: 'I'll go with him.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ron to canvass other department heads to find out who's testifying.
jokes.punchline: Ron has worked at city hall for years and simply doesn't know anyone else's name. He states this without shame.
jokes.explanation: Ron's deliberate isolation from his colleagues is a core character trait deployed for a good quick laugh. The beat where Ann immediately volunteers to go with him is the perfect reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I need you to be honest with me, but also tell me what I want to hear.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Those are the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No they're not!

jokes.text: Leslie asks Ann to 'text me every 30 seconds that everything's gonna be okay.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is delegating tasks to her team before the trial resumes.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of '30 seconds' — not 'regularly,' not 'every few minutes' — reveals the true depth of Leslie's anxiety and her absolute faith in Ann's role as emotional support.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '30 seconds' is what elevates this above a generic 'keep me posted' gag. It's absurd but also completely believable for Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The subject line was 'yay' with forty-seven Y's and eighty-three exclamation points.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'But when you sit back and let your reputation be destroyed, you go down in history as a frozen whore.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining her decision to fight the charges rather than simply accept punishment.
jokes.punchline: 'You go down in history as a frozen whore' — the specific, vivid, historically-flavored insult is the comedic payload, delivered with complete conviction.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable. 'Frozen whore' as Leslie's specific fear — rooted in the Sarah Nelson Quindle callback (set adrift like a human popsicle) — is both a funny phrase and subtly a callback to her earlier historical analogy. The righteous fury with which Leslie delivers it makes it land even harder.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: In a world... where one woman dared to dream bigger than anyone thought possible... where she fought for what she believed in... where she never gave up... even when the odds were against her...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant!

jokes.text: Leslie asks Ann about Ben: 'You need to cheer him up, Ann.' Ann: 'Ben is fine.' Then: 'He said to look at the monster. I'm hoping you know what that means.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is worried about Ben waiting outside.
jokes.punchline: Ann relays Ben's message about 'the monster' with genuine confusion — not knowing the context of Ben's earlier self-deprecating joke.
jokes.explanation: Good callback structure. Ann's baffled delivery of 'I'm hoping you know what that means' is the punchline — the audience has the context she doesn't, which creates a nice comedic gap.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm equally excited about learning iMovie.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Just make sure he can't talk.' / Ann: (beat) / Leslie: 'Wait. Let me make it clear. Don't silence him. Just make sure he can't talk.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to neutralize a potential witness and catches herself sounding like she's ordering a hit.
jokes.punchline: Her 'correction' — 'Don't silence him. Just make sure he can't talk' — is functionally identical to what she just said, revealing she doesn't understand why it was alarming.
jokes.explanation: Excellent construction. The initial line is alarming, the retraction seems like it will clarify, but the 'correction' is semantically identical. Leslie doesn't realize this because in her mind they ARE different (one is sinister, one is just... practical). The joke works on a logical level AND a character level. Quotable and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie? Oh, she's a great employee. Very... on-brand.

jokes.text: The 'yay' email subject line: 'Y-A and 18 Y's and 44 exclamation points.'
jokes.setup: Leslie directs Ann to an email in her inbox as evidence of when the relationship began.
jokes.punchline: The subject line: 'Y-A and 18 Y's and 44 exclamation points' — an exact count that implies someone actually counted, revealing the depth of Leslie's enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 44 exclamation points tells you everything about Leslie Knope's emotional register. The joke is in the detail and the implication that someone (Leslie, or possibly a committee member) counted all of them.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: So, are you and Leslie lovers?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! No! We're not— I mean, she's married to Ben. We're just friends and colleagues.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I was just asking a simple question.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, don't use that word. 'Lovers' sounds so... European and weird.

jokes.text: The iMovie trailer Leslie made about her and Ben's relationship — 'In a world on the brink of financial meltdown... An adorable man with a cute face and the future president of the United States...went from being friends to being so much more.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has submitted as evidence an email attachment — which turns out to be a romantic movie trailer she made about herself and Ben using iMovie.
jokes.punchline: The trailer is played in open court, narrated in full movie-trailer dramatic style, describing Ben as 'an adorable man with a cute face' and Leslie as 'the future president of the United States—what?'
jokes.explanation: Leslie made a movie trailer for her own romance using iMovie. This is so specific, so perfectly Leslie, and so mortifying in the context of a formal ethics hearing that it's one of the episode's highlights. The 'future president of the United States—what?' self-insert is particularly great — Leslie's ambition smuggled into her romantic fantasy. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie and I never dated because she's like a beautiful, ambitious, hard-working golden retriever, and I'm like a possum that plays dead when things get difficult.

jokes.text: The voicemail/video attachment: 'Ann! Ben and I hooked up last night! Aah! And I learned how to use iMovie. Call me later! Bye!'
jokes.setup: The iMovie trailer has just played in open court.
jokes.punchline: The attachment ends with Leslie's excited video message where she celebrates BOTH the hookup AND learning iMovie with equal enthusiasm — now playing for a formal ethics committee.
jokes.explanation: The equal billing given to learning iMovie and hooking up with Ben is perfectly Leslie. The cringe is maximized because this is playing to an ethics tribunal. 'And I learned how to use iMovie' as a co-equal announcement with a romantic milestone is a wonderful character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: Your Honor, I've known Leslie Knope for years, and she's the most dedicated public servant I know.

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: Thank you. Do you have anything else to add?

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: Well, I would, but honestly, I blame the court stenographer for everything that's gone wrong in my life. My divorce, my job loss, my baldness — all her fault.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Mr. Haverford, would you consider Leslie Knope a good employee?' / Tom: 'Did Tom Ford turn around the House of Gucci?' / Chris: 'I do not know, but I'll assume that that is a yes.'
jokes.setup: Chris asks Tom a simple yes/no question about Leslie's performance.
jokes.punchline: Tom answers with an obscure fashion industry reference as if it's obvious, and Chris — who is aggressively healthy and positive but has no pop culture frame — just decides to assume yes.
jokes.explanation: Two-character comedy: Tom's inability to give a straight answer even in a legal setting, and Chris's earnest literalism. 'I do not know, but I'll assume that that is a yes' is a very Chris line — methodical, positive, slightly out of his depth.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I'm gonna hold myself in contempt of court!

jokes.text: Chris: 'How long were you two lovers?' / Tom: 'Excuse me?' — The implication that Tom and Leslie had a relationship.
jokes.setup: Chris has seemingly discovered evidence of Leslie kissing Tom.
jokes.punchline: Tom's completely genuine 'Excuse me?' — the shock of being accused of being Leslie's lover.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the longer Tom/Leslie sequence. The 'Excuse me?' is a simple but well-timed reaction beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I didn't do it. But while I'm under oath, I should probably mention I stole a laptop from the office in 2009 and spilled spaghetti all over it.

jokes.text: Tom's explanation of why they kissed: 'An online dating site randomly paired us up. So, as a joke, I thought it would be funny to pretend you and I were dating. And then you kissed me as a joke... to shut me up.'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining the innocent context of the kiss that Chris has just weaponized.
jokes.punchline: The increasingly ridiculous chain of events — random pairing, fake dating, kiss-to-shut-him-up — that led to this moment being used as courtroom evidence.
jokes.explanation: The absurd specificity of the chain of events is funny. Leslie kissing Tom 'to shut him up' is a great character detail — it sounds rude but is entirely plausible for their dynamic.

jokes.text: Tom: 'No, that would be like dating my older sister's elderly aunt.' / Leslie: 'No, it wouldn't.'
jokes.setup: Tom is asked if he had any other romantic contact with Leslie after the kiss.
jokes.punchline: Tom's insult disguised as a clarification — 'my older sister's elderly aunt' — and Leslie's flat, simple rebuttal.
jokes.explanation: Two lines, maximum efficiency. Tom's specific hierarchy — not just 'an aunt' but 'my older sister's elderly aunt' — makes it funnier. Leslie's 'No, it wouldn't' is the perfect understated wounded response. The joke earns its score through sheer economy.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I may have thrown a TV out the window. But that's just because I got mad at the ending of a Lifetime movie.

jokes.text: Character witness Ethel Beavers interrupting to say: 'I don't know why Leslie Knope's on trial. Ethel Beavers did it!' then 'I will hold myself in contempt of court!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is presenting character witnesses, and the elderly court stenographer Ethel Beavers has apparently been called.
jokes.punchline: Ethel Beavers confesses to something unknown, then threatens to hold herself in contempt — a procedural concept she clearly doesn't understand.
jokes.explanation: Ethel is a recurring bit character and her chaotic energy here is perfectly deployed. 'I will hold myself in contempt of court!' is particularly good — it's legally nonsensical in the funniest way. The specificity of 'Ethel Beavers did it!' without any context for what she did is peak absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I crushed it in there. I've watched every episode of Law & Order: SVU. I basically know everything about the legal system.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's not how any of this works.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ice-T agrees with me.

jokes.text: Leslie's reaction to Tom's 'older sister's elderly aunt' comparison: 'No, it wouldn't.'
jokes.setup: Tom says dating Leslie would be like dating his older sister's elderly aunt.
jokes.punchline: Leslie objects to the specific framing of the analogy, not the underlying sentiment — she's offended by the phrasing rather than the implication. The flat 'No, it wouldn't.' is perfectly Leslie.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly placed. The joke is maximally economic — 'No, it wouldn't' says everything. Leslie's objection to the logical accuracy of the analogy (rather than the insult) is her pedantry and self-regard colliding. Maximum economy score (10) because you couldn't say this in fewer words.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your Honor, I stand before you today to defend the integrity of our parks and the grants— I mean, the... the grands...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No wait, grants. G-R-A—

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: Ms. Knope, are you quite finished?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I just... I had this whole thing planned and now I've ruined the entire moment by not knowing how to say a basic word that I use constantly in my job.

jokes.text: A character (likely Jerry/Gary) confesses to accidentally taking a work laptop home: 'Is this about the laptop? I didn't mean to steal it. I took it home, and I spaced... It totally works, but I got spaghetti in the keyboard.'
jokes.setup: In the middle of the ethics trial, someone appears to randomly confess to something entirely unrelated.
jokes.punchline: 'It totally works, but I got spaghetti in the keyboard' — the specific detail of spaghetti makes this a perfect Jerry moment: embarrassing, mundane, and completely beside the point.
jokes.explanation: The spaghetti detail is what makes this great. Jerry/Gary confessing to a minor laptop theft during an ethics trial is a perfect Parks background character moment. 'I got spaghetti in the keyboard' is so specific and so Jerry — a man for whom things simply go wrong in mundane domestic ways.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ethel, I'm concerned about you betting on the town election. That raises serious ethical questions.

dialogue.speaker: Ethel
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're literally on trial for ethics violations.

jokes.text: After the laptop confession: the committee chair says 'What laptop?' and Leslie says 'Objection.'
jokes.setup: A random laptop confession has derailed the proceedings.
jokes.punchline: The committee chair's confused 'What laptop?' — as if even they don't know what's happening — followed by Leslie's instinctive 'Objection' which makes no sense in context.
jokes.explanation: Quick button on the laptop gag. Leslie's reflexive 'Objection' when she's the one on trial is a nice absurdist touch — she's just been watching too much Law & Order (which Donna references later).

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't have an address. I have a series of unmarked dirt roads and a hand-drawn map that I destroyed after committing it to memory.

dialogue.speaker: Judge/Lawyer
dialogue.line: Sir, we need your address for the court record.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're welcome to try and find it. Many have tried. All have failed. I've hidden my cabin so well that I can barely find it myself.

jokes.text: Donna describes what Leslie and Ben were wearing as 'your basic white people clothes' — 'khakis and button-down shirts.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Donna to describe what they were wearing to establish no romantic atmosphere was present.
jokes.punchline: 'Your basic white people clothes' as the clinical descriptor for the outfits.
jokes.explanation: Pure Donna. Her blunt racial observation is delivered with complete comfort — it's funny because it's true and because it's exactly how Donna would describe khakis. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I need your address for the official record.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Beep beep beep beep beep beep beep

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 42 Ramsett Point Road!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Beep beep beep beep beep beep beep beep beep

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 42 RAMSETT POINT ROAD, PAWNEE, INDIANA!

jokes.text: Donna: 'I have ruined my share of hotel rooms, and trust me, nothing sexual happened in that room. It kind of looked like an office.'
jokes.setup: Donna is testifying that the hotel room looked businesslike, not romantic.
jokes.punchline: 'I have ruined my share of hotel rooms' — a confession of past behavior delivered with zero shame as her credential for recognizing non-sexual hotel rooms.
jokes.explanation: Donna establishing her expertise by offhandedly referencing her extensive history of ruined hotel rooms is excellent character comedy. The confidence with which she says this — as an unimpeachable credential — is the joke. 'Trust me, nothing sexual happened in that room' as the conclusion only she could reach, based only on evidence she's uniquely positioned to evaluate. Highly quotable. One of the episode's best Donna moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy Two is a demon. Literally a demon. I'm not speaking figuratively or hyperbolically. I mean that she is actually a demon from Hell.

jokes.text: Donna's talking head: 'I've seen over 200 episodes of Law & Order, and it's paying off big-time.'
jokes.setup: Donna is reflecting on her role helping Leslie in the trial.
jokes.punchline: She attributes her legal aptitude entirely to binge-watching Law & Order — not law school, not experience — 200 episodes.
jokes.explanation: Funny Donna character beat. The specific count of '200 episodes' rather than 'a lot of Law & Order' elevates this — it implies she has been tracking. The confidence in this credential is pure Donna.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I have evidence that will destroy you.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Tammy, if you release that, I will never come to another Sweetums event.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: You wouldn't dare.

jokes.text: Leslie asks the court stenographer Ethel about her trial odds. Ethel: 'I'd say it's 50/50.' Then: 'You want to put money on it, I'll give you 60/40 against.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is seeking reassurance from a veteran of the process.
jokes.punchline: Ethel gives a neutral assessment then immediately reveals she's willing to bet — at worse odds — implying she has a private opinion she hasn't shared.
jokes.explanation: Ethel's pivot from neutral analyst to shady gambler in two lines is well-constructed. The follow-up — 'Is it ethical for a court stenographer to bet on the outcome of a hearing?' / 'You tell me. You're the one on trial.' — is excellent. The second line is the real punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, he's just a maintenance worker. He's not important. Nobody cares about him.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not like he's gonna go to the police or anything. I mean, I've done worse things than that.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Is it ethical for a court stenographer to bet on the outcome of a hearing?' / Ethel: 'You tell me. You're the one on trial.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to call out Ethel's betting as itself unethical.
jokes.punchline: Ethel deflects back with 'You tell me. You're the one on trial.' — completely unapologetic and turning the question back on Leslie.
jokes.explanation: This is Ethel's best moment. 'You tell me. You're the one on trial.' is a devastatingly well-constructed comeback — it simultaneously dodges the question, reminds Leslie of her position, and establishes Ethel as having zero interest in her own accountability. Perfect economy. The confidence of the delivery makes it land hard.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: Yes, I used the spa gift certificate. I got a facial and let me tell you, my skin has never felt better. It was wonderful.

jokes.text: Ron on the stand refuses to give his cabin address, saying 'Ah!' every time Leslie or anyone gets close to saying it out loud.
jokes.setup: Leslie needs Ron to confirm he owns a cabin at a specific address — the address is relevant evidence.
jokes.punchline: Ron interrupts with increasingly desperate 'Ah!' sounds every time anyone is about to say his address out loud in an official record.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences. Ron's libertarian privacy obsession, already established in the cold open, comes to a perfect head here. The escalating 'Ah! / Beep! / Ah!' sounds — Ron literally trying to audibly censor himself in formal proceedings — is physical comedy through dialogue. The final 'I didn't hear that' as she eventually shouts the address is a great button. Peak character integration: this joke only exists because of Ron Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: I can't read this without my glasses.

dialogue.speaker: George
dialogue.line: Wait, it says 'If you can't read this, you're too blind to read.'

jokes.text: Ron: 'I can smell the sulfur coming off her cloven hooves.' (about Tammy Two's arrival)
jokes.setup: Ron senses his ex-wife Tammy Two has arrived.
jokes.punchline: He describes her approach using the language of demonic possession — 'sulfur,' 'cloven hooves' — completely matter-of-factly.
jokes.explanation: Ron's absolute conviction that his ex-wife is literally demonic, delivered with his characteristic stoicism, is excellent character work. 'Sulfur coming off her cloven hooves' is vivid and specific — not generic 'she's a monster' but full mythological imagery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need time to research my defense. I'm going to need a recess.

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: How long?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Twelve years.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Tammy Two is your killer witness? Please! You're gonna have to do better—' / Chris: '—Actually, she is a terrifying sociopath who could say or do anything—' / Leslie: 'A pretty good killer witness.'
jokes.setup: Leslie dismisses Tammy Two as a witness. Chris begins to agree, then pivots.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate reversal — 'A pretty good killer witness' — as she realizes mid-sentence she has no leg to stand on.
jokes.explanation: Good rapid reversal comedy. The structure is three lines but the timing has to be perfect — Leslie's bluster collapses in real time. The callback to the established 'killer witness' question gives it context.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Why does my book not have any pictures? I specifically asked for the pop-up version.

jokes.text: Chris warns Tammy: 'May I remind you that you are under oath, and if you lie, I will fire you and have you prosecuted.' Tammy pivots instantly: 'Nothing. They will definitively prove nothing. You cut me off.'
jokes.setup: Tammy is about to present damning evidence against Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Chris's threat of prosecution causes Tammy to instantly reverse her entire testimony — 'You cut me off.' Delivered with zero shame.
jokes.explanation: Tammy's complete reversal of testimony under mild legal threat, then blaming Chris for 'cutting her off,' is brilliant character work. The pivot happens in real time and the audience sees exactly what she's doing. 'You cut me off' as a shameless non-excuse is the perfect Tammy move. Great structure: build, threat, instant collapse, brazen deflection.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: In 1631, it was illegal to kiss your wife on Sunday. In 1662, it was illegal to kiss your wife on any day. By 1687, it was just illegal to have a wife.

jokes.text: Tammy: 'Oh, Chris—so silly. Okay, bye, guys. Leslie, have fun with this trial. Yay!'
jokes.setup: Tammy has just completely reversed her testimony and is now leaving.
jokes.punchline: She departs with the breezy insincerity of someone leaving a brunch — 'Yay!' — as if none of the chaos she caused was her problem.
jokes.explanation: Good button on Tammy's appearance. The 'Yay!' is perfectly sociopathic — genuine or ironic, it doesn't matter, it's wrong for every reason.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh man, check this out. There's this old law still on the books that's just... wow, this is really dark.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I can't believe nobody's done anything about this. It's just sitting there, making us all look terrible.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head mid-trial: 'George Williams? Who's—' [PAUSE] 'Oh, George Williams — he's just a maintenance worker, NASCAR enthusiast, I believe. And, oh, interesting tidbit — I once bribed him to keep my relationship with Ben quiet.'
jokes.setup: Leslie starts confused by the name, then gradually remembers who he is, then remembers something important she had not previously disclosed.
jokes.punchline: The casual escalation: NASCAR enthusiast → 'interesting tidbit' → 'I once bribed him' — delivered with the tone of someone mentioning an amusing coincidence rather than a bombshell confession.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best-constructed joke. The structure is immaculate: (1) genuine confusion, (2) slow recognition, (3) perfectly calibrated 'interesting tidbit' as a frame for what is actually case-ending information. Leslie's brain making this connection in real time, on camera, in front of the committee, is perfectly realized. The phrase 'interesting tidbit' doing maximum damage with minimum words is exactly what great comedy writing looks like. The pause between the two sections is where the joke lives. Justifiably the episode's highest score.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: According to this 1887 municipal code, a woman can't leave her house without her husband's permission or a signed letter from him.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow. That's... actually not a terrible idea.

jokes.text: George Williams testifies: Leslie gave him a $50 gift certificate to a spa, and he got a facial. 'My wife said my skin was luminous.'
jokes.setup: George is testifying about the bribe — Leslie and Ben paid him to stay quiet about seeing them kiss.
jokes.punchline: The bribe was a $50 spa gift certificate, and his main takeaway from the whole incident is that his skin looked great afterward.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'my wife said my skin was luminous' — George's complete contentment with the bribe and his pride in the outcome — is a great detail. It humanizes the 'bribery' as completely benign while making it legally incriminating for Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're not a bad person. You're just a person who does bad things sometimes. We all do. The difference between you and most people is that you feel bad about it, which is annoying, but also kind of admirable.

jokes.text: Leslie's attempt to undermine George's testimony with a glasses gambit: 'I don't recall you wearing glasses. Could it be because you weren't wearing glasses?' George: 'I never wear 'em on the job.' Leslie: 'Can you take your glasses off, please, and read this for us?' George reads: 'I could read this if I weren't so blind.' / Leslie: 'Well, that went terribly.'
jokes.setup: Leslie, improvising in the courtroom, tries a Perry Mason-style glasses-based credibility attack on the witness.
jokes.punchline: The sign she hands him for the 'reading test' says 'I could read this if I weren't so blind' — pre-prepared, meaning she had this plan, and it still failed spectacularly. Her self-assessment: 'Well, that went terribly.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe escalation. What makes this special is that the glasses gambit was clearly premeditated — she had the sign ready — but she failed to account for the possibility that George can actually read without glasses. The prepared sign saying 'I could read this if I weren't so blind' is itself a great absurdist detail. Leslie's flat 'Well, that went terribly' is a perfect self-aware button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I let everyone down. I'm so sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Are you kidding me? This is the proudest I've ever been of you. You bent the rules, cut some corners, maybe broke a few laws. That's not failure, Leslie—that's growth.

jokes.text: Andy about one of the old legal books: 'Okay, mine doesn't have any pictures.'
jokes.setup: The team is frantically searching old municipal law books for a loophole to help Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Andy's contribution to the research effort is noting the absence of pictures — implying that without pictures, he hasn't been engaging with the content.
jokes.explanation: Quick Andy character beat. The joke is obvious but executed with perfect economy and strong character fit. Not a highlight but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie really wounded me to the core. I've been doing core exercises all week and my abs are killing me.

jokes.text: From the old law books: 'In 1856, the city council banned all sexual positions except for missionary. And two years later, they banned missionary.'
jokes.setup: The team is reading archaic municipal laws in search of a useful statute.
jokes.punchline: Pawnee banned missionary two years after banning everything else — implying a sequential legislative campaign to ban all human sexuality.
jokes.explanation: Classic Pawnee historical absurdism at its best. The two-step structure — ban all positions except missionary, then ban missionary — is perfectly constructed. The two-year gap implies a genuine legislative process was involved in banning all sex. Highly quotable, unexpected, and earns its score through structure and dark wit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Can you please stop jumping? We're having a serious conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I can't help it. Jumping is how I manage my depression.

jokes.text: '1882, should a Presbyterian speak out of turn, he may be caned across the shinbone.'
jokes.setup: More archaic Pawnee laws being read aloud.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'Presbyterian' and 'shinbone' — not just 'beaten' but specifically caned on that specific bone — gives this an unusually precise absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The double specificity of 'Presbyterian' and 'shinbone' is what makes this work. Both details are funnier than more generic alternatives would have been. Part of a strong comedic sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Was it worth it? All the trouble?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: 'Black people still can't legally use city sidewalks.'
jokes.setup: The team continues to find appalling historical laws.
jokes.punchline: The flat delivery of a law that is not historical at all — it's framed as still current — is the darkest beat in the episode.
jokes.explanation: Parks and Recreation's use of Pawnee's racist history is pointed here — the present tense makes it darker than the preceding laws. The comedic device (reading bad old laws) lands with more bite here. The lack of a reaction from anyone in the scene is itself a comment on how normalized it is in Pawnee's culture.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: *deep breath* That was... that was really beautiful, Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: Chris made several emotional sounds: a whimper, a sigh, and what could only be described as a sustained moan of appreciation.

jokes.text: 'Any woman caught laughing is a witch.' Followed by someone responding: 'That's true.'
jokes.setup: The law-reading sequence continues.
jokes.punchline: 'That's true.' — an offhand agreement with the law about laughing women being witches.
jokes.explanation: The 'That's true' button is what elevates this above the preceding law-reading gags. Someone in the room casually co-signing misogynist witch law is a sharp quick joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Actually, my name isn't Jerry. It's Garry. With two Rs and no 'J'. But everyone's called me Jerry for so long, I didn't want to be rude and correct you all.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, so your name is Garry?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, technically it's Gareth. But like I said, I've just gotten used to Jerry.

jokes.text: The mural 'Bad Pawnee, Good Pawnee': Leslie discovers she's on the bad side.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron are having a serious conversation near a mural depicting Pawnee's history.
jokes.punchline: Leslie realizes she appears on the 'bad' side of the mural — a visual confirmation of her self-perceived moral failure in the moment of her lowest point.
jokes.explanation: Good visual/thematic joke — the mural placement is both funny (Pawnee's murals are always absurdist) and genuinely lands emotionally because it hits at Leslie's lowest moment. The show earns this kind of joke by having established the mural tradition.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, your name is Gary? Gary Gergich?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's somehow worse than Jerry. I'm gonna keep calling you Jerry.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Bribing someone to hide a sexcapade — I'm proud to call you a friend.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just confessed to bribing George and is apologizing to her team.
jokes.punchline: Tom's reversal — this revelation has made him MORE impressed with Leslie, not less.
jokes.explanation: Tom's value system being precisely calibrated to appreciate bribery for romantic concealment is very on-brand. 'Sexcapade' is a very Tom word. 'I'm proud to call you a friend' as genuine admiration rather than irony is the unexpected angle.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I... I need a minute. I need to process this information about Gary. This is... this is a lot to take in right now.

jokes.text: Chris's farewell to Leslie: 'Your actions wounded me to my core, which is not easy since the bulk of my workouts are focused on core strengthening.'
jokes.setup: Chris is giving a heartfelt speech about how Leslie's bribery hurt him personally.
jokes.punchline: The pivot from emotional 'wounded me to my core' to literal core workouts — Chris cannot help himself.
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best jokes. The wordplay on 'core' (emotional core / core muscles) is perfectly organic — it sounds like the kind of thing Chris would genuinely think and then be unable to not say. The structure is beautiful: emotionally earnest setup → physical fitness non-sequitur → quick return to sincerity. Only Chris Traeger could say this line. Very high character integration. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: The trial transcript: 'Mr. Wyatt: Chris, for God's sake, would you mind not jumping for a while?' / 'Mr. Traeger: Sorry, Ben, but this is how I fight depression. Okay, fine. I'll stop. Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is reading the transcript of Ben's private meeting with the ethics committee.
jokes.punchline: Even during a meeting where Ben is resigning and professing love for Leslie, Chris is jumping — and Ben has to ask him to stop mid-meeting.
jokes.explanation: The joke requires knowing Chris's jumping habit is his defense against depression — a great callback. The transcript format makes it funnier: 'Mr. Traeger: Sorry, Ben, but this is how I fight depression. Okay, fine. I'll stop. Thank you.' The formality of the transcript capturing Chris's wellness rituals is excellent. 'Crying noise, crying noise, nose blow' in the transcript moments later continues this joke beautifully.

jokes.text: The transcript ends with: 'Mr. Traeger: That was beautiful. I'm literally crying and jumping. Crying noise, crying noise, nose blow. Mr. Wyatt: It's gonna be okay. Mr. Traeger: ...' [Oh.]
jokes.setup: Ben has just declared his love for Leslie in the official transcript.
jokes.punchline: The transcript dutifully records Chris's emotional reaction: 'Crying noise, crying noise, nose blow.' — sounds formally entered into an official government record.
jokes.explanation: This might be the episode's most perfectly executed joke. 'Crying noise, crying noise, nose blow' as official government testimony — formally recorded by the stenographer — is brilliant on multiple levels. It works as character comedy (Chris crying), as meta comedy (the formalism of transcribing sounds), and as emotional comedy (the context is a love declaration). The economy is extraordinary: three words do the work of a whole scene. 'End transcript.' as the button is perfect. This is genuinely exceptional television comedy writing — earns its score.

jokes.text: Leslie formally reopens the record to state her love for Ben, with Ethel narrating: 'The official record has now annoyingly been reopened so that Leslie Knope can make a statement.'
jokes.setup: Leslie wants the record to reflect her love for Ben and has Ethel reopen the official transcript.
jokes.punchline: Ethel's editorial aside — 'annoyingly been reopened' — inserted right into official government record language.
jokes.explanation: Ethel using 'annoyingly' in formal government language is a great character beat — she can't suppress her personal opinion even in her professional function. The joke also serves as a warm comedic frame for a genuinely romantic moment, which is exactly what the show does best.

jokes.text: After the love declaration scene, Ethel asks: 'Can I get a ride home? It's freezing.'
jokes.setup: A genuinely emotional romantic moment has just concluded.
jokes.punchline: Ethel immediately cuts the sentiment completely by asking for a ride home.
jokes.explanation: Perfect tonal cut. The episode has just had a real emotional peak, and Ethel's 'Can I get a ride home? It's freezing.' is the best possible button — utterly practical, completely unromantic. Economy is nearly perfect: six words that immediately deflate the moment without undermining it. This is a master class in scene-ending comedy.

jokes.text: The Gary/Jerry revelation: his real name is Gary, but he never corrected his boss because 'I just didn't think I should correct him.' The team reacts with increasing disbelief.
jokes.setup: Gary/Jerry is called to testify. He gives his name as Gary Gergich.
jokes.punchline: Everyone has called him Jerry for years. His real name is Gary. He let it happen for his entire tenure because he didn't want to correct the director.
jokes.explanation: This is a revelation-level joke and one of the show's great character moments. The setup has been years of 'Jerry' being everyone's punching bag — and now we learn not even his NAME is right, and he silently accepted the wrong name his entire career because he didn't want to make waves. It's simultaneously hilarious and quietly devastating. The character integration is as high as it goes — this could only work for this character. The team's reactions compound it beautifully.

jokes.text: The group tries out 'Gary Gergich' and 'Jerry Gergich' back and forth, concluding both are horrible — but deciding to stick with Jerry.
jokes.setup: The committee tries to process that his name is actually Gary.
jokes.punchline: They conclude both names are awful ('Gary Gergich. Jerry Gergich. Gary Gergich. Jerry— God, they're both horrible.') but choose to keep calling him Jerry because 'Jerry's better.'
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff to the reveal. The committee doesn't choose the correct name — they choose the wrong name because it sounds slightly better. Jerry will continue to be called the wrong name. The cruelty is casual and complete. 'That's ridiculous. Your name is Jerry. No. Legally my name is Gary.' is a great exchange, and 'I'm gonna call you Jerry' seals his fate with absolute authority.

jokes.text: 'Gary Gergich? Jerry Gergich. Gary Gergich. Jerry Gergich. Gary Gergich. Jerry— God, they're both horrible. But Jerry's better. I'm gonna call you Jerry.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is processing the name revelation.
jokes.punchline: After genuine deliberation, she decides that 'Jerry' is actually better than 'Gary' and will continue calling him the wrong name — with full awareness that it's wrong.
jokes.explanation: The follow-through on the Gary/Jerry joke is even funnier than the reveal. Leslie genuinely deliberating — 'Gary Gergich. Jerry Gergich' — and landing on 'they're both horrible. But Jerry's better' before doubling down on the wrong name is a perfect comedic payoff. It transforms what could have been a redemptive moment for Jerry/Gary into an escalation of his eternal bad luck. The show's affectionate cruelty toward this character at its finest.

jokes.text: Chris: 'I'm sorry. I can't get over the Gary/Jerry thing.' / Committee member: 'Neither can I. Jerry, you can go. We need a five-minute break.'
jokes.setup: The Gary/Jerry revelation has effectively ended the proceedings.
jokes.punchline: Even the official committee needs a five-minute break to process the name situation — the entire room has been derailed by Jerry's existence.
jokes.explanation: The committee needing a recess due to a witness's name is an absurd but perfect escalation. 'Jerry, you can go' — dismissing him by the wrong name even after the revelation — is a great button. The episode ending on this note (with the sync tag following) is a strong comedic choice.

tmdb_overview: Leslie has to face an ethics committee about her secret relationship with Ben after they come clean to Chris.
insight: Trial courtroom setting grounds absurdist chaos in character-driven mockery.
